title: A well-made head
hook: better a well-made head than a well-filled one (Essays 1.26)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was just custom: the woman who carried a calf until it was an ox. Your line was just custom.

A trivia night at a bar. One team has a member who knows every capital, every element, every year a war ended. They win. Later that week, the same person is asked to help a friend decide whether to take a job in another city, and has nothing to offer but more facts. A head can be very full and still not very useful. In a long essay on how to raise a child, Montaigne draws exactly this line, in one plain phrase.
screen: `A WINNING TRIVIA TEAM.` → `NO HELP WITH A REAL CHOICE.` → `FULL, BUT NOT USEFUL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When choosing a tutor for a child, Montaigne says, look for one with a well-made head rather than a well-filled one. Both would be good, he allows, but character and understanding matter more than learning. Second, the funnel. Teachers, he complains, keep shouting into children's ears as if pouring into a funnel, and the child's only job is to repeat what was said. He wants the opposite: let the student taste things, choose, and tell them apart. Sometimes the tutor opens the way; sometimes he lets the student open it. And he puts it bluntly: knowing something by heart is not knowing it. Third, the bees. Bees go from flower to flower taking what they like, but the honey they make is all their own; it's no longer thyme or marjoram. A student should do the same with what they borrow from books: turn it into their own judgment. Fourth, the test. How do you know someone has learned? Not by what they can recite. By how they live. Montaigne has a homely picture for it: if food comes back up just as it went down, it was never digested. Learning that comes out word for word hasn't been taken in. Away from the classroom, a well-made head can belong to the friend who knows few capitals but asks the one question that helps you decide.
screen: `WELL MADE, NOT WELL FILLED.` · `NOT A FUNNEL.` · `BEES MAKE THEIR OWN HONEY.` · `PROOF IS IN HOW YOU LIVE.` · then, large: `WELL MADE, NOT FULL.`

segments.voice: Pick one idea from these days on the path that you could recite but maybe couldn't explain: water, the runaway horse, custom, different roads. Put it in your own words, in your head, as if telling a twelve-year-old at the kitchen table, with no quoting. If it falls apart, that's useful too; try again, plainer.
A well-made head. Montaigne's picture of a good mind: not stuffed with facts, but able to judge, like bees turning flowers into honey of their own. Today's word.
Your line: well made, not full. The honey belongs to the bees, whatever flowers it came from. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay on the education of children take its line about a well-made head as a case for teaching judgment over memorization.

chat.says: My kid memorizes everything for tests. Isn't that what good learning looks like?
options: Montaigne says knowing by heart isn't knowing; learning shows in judgment and life.
Montaigne says yes: a well-filled head is the surest sign a child has learned.
Montaigne says skip books entirely, since children learn only by playing outside.
chat.meaning: Montaigne wants a well-made head rather than a well-filled one. Like bees making their own honey, learning becomes judgment, and the proof is how you live.

Montaigne.meaning: Michel de Montaigne, French nobleman who wrote the Essays

notes: Essays 1.26 (path numbering; 1.25 in some English editions) paraphrased throughout. Montaigne's French: 'plutôt la tête bien faite que bien pleine'; 'savoir par cœur n'est pas savoir'. Confirm.
The essay is addressed to a noblewoman about her expected child; the script leaves out the name.
Montaigne writes of the pupil as a boy; the script uses 'the student' and 'the child' and keeps 'teach himself' only in a fork option.
